nodes.name: Continuous-time random walk (CTRW) with drift $X_t$
nodes.statement: By this we understand a random process $X_t$ whose evolution in time can be thought of as the result of the combined effect of a constant drift and the occurrence of random jumps. Thus, for $t\geqslant t_0$ we define \begin{equation} X_t=X_{t_0}+v(t-t_0)+S_{t}, \quad S_t=\sum_{n=1}^\infty J_n\ \theta(t-t_n), \end{equation} where $\theta(u)=1$ for $u \geqslant 0$, $t_n=\tau_1+\cdots+\tau_n$ are the jump times, $J_n$ the jump magnitude and $v>0$ by convention.
nodes.statement_short: A CTRW with drift: a constant drift $v(t-t_0)$ plus a compound jump term $S_t=\sum_n J_n\theta(t-t_n)$.
differentia: the result of the combined effect of a constant drift and the occurrence of random jumps

nodes.name: Standing assumptions on sojourn times and jump magnitudes
nodes.statement: All through this paper we will assume that (i) the sojourn times $\tau_n>0$ are independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) random variables with probability density and cumulative distribution function (PDF and, respectively, CDF) $\psi(t)$ and $\Psi(t)= \int_0^t \psi(t')d t'$; (ii) $\{J_n\}$ is a sequence of i.i.d. random variables with common PDF $h(\cdot)$; and (iii), that $ J_m$ is independent of $\tau_n $ for any $n,m$.
nodes.statement_short: Sojourn times are i.i.d. with PDF/CDF $\psi,\Psi$, jumps are i.i.d. with PDF $h$, and jumps are independent of sojourn times.

nodes.name: Compound Poisson process (CPP) limit of a drift-less CTRW
nodes.statement: In absence of drift, and when the holding times $\tau_n$ are exponentially distributed, $\tau_n\sim \mathcal E(\lambda)$ for some $\lambda >0$, the jump process $S_t$ is a classical compound Poisson process (CPP) characterized by having independent increments $S_{t+h}- S_t$; in addition the associated ``arrival-process'' $N_t\equiv\sum_{n=1}^\infty \theta(t-t_n)$ is Poisson distributed: $N_t \sim \mathcal P(\lambda t)$.
nodes.statement_short: With exponential holding times and no drift the jump process is a compound Poisson process with Poisson counting process.
assumptions: In absence of drift, and when the holding times $\tau_n$ are exponentially distributed, $\tau_n\sim \mathcal E(\lambda)$ for some $\lambda >0$
conclusions: the jump process $S_t$ is a classical compound Poisson process (CPP) characterized by having independent increments $S_{t+h}- S_t$
the associated ``arrival-process'' $N_t\equiv\sum_{n=1}^\infty \theta(t-t_n)$ is Poisson distributed: $N_t \sim \mathcal P(\lambda t)$

nodes.name: Mean exit time from $(0,b)$ of a drifting CTRW given only the present state
nodes.statement: here we pose the problem of evaluating the mean exit time from the interval $(0,b)$ of a drifting CTRW $X_t$ when {\it the only available information is the present state\/} $X_r=x$, where $r \geqslant 0$ is the present chronological time |note that, by adjusting the time clock and spatial scale, the results carry over to any interval $(a,b)$ and initial time $t_0$.
nodes.statement_short: Compute the mean exit time of a drifting CTRW from $(0,b)$ when only the present state $X_r=x$ is known.

nodes.name: Prior drift-less results do not extend to a generic non-Markovian CTRW
nodes.statement: We note however that these results do not cover a generic situation. Indeed, while for CPPs (as for the general L\'evy processes) Markov property implies that results derived starting at a jump time carry over to arbitrary present, no such inference is possible for a generic CTRW due to its non-Markovian nature. Thus, escape times \it depend on the actual state and available information \rm and hence the question as to how to generalize the former results to \it general present time \rm $r$ appears naturally.
nodes.statement_short: Because a generic CTRW is non-Markovian, results derived at a jump instant do not carry over to an arbitrary present time.

nodes.name: Effect of dropping the assumption that the present is a jump time
nodes.statement: In particular, it remains an open question to what extent dropping the assumption that ``the present is a jump time'' affects the relevant probabilities.
nodes.statement_short: To what extent does dropping ``the present is a jump time'' change the relevant probabilities?

nodes.name: Erlang distribution $\mathcal Er(\lambda,n)$
nodes.statement: $\mathcal Er(\lambda,n)$ corresponds to having a sum of $n$ independent exponential variables and hence generalizes the exponential density in a natural way, \begin{equation} \psi(t) = \frac{\lambda^n t^{n-1}}{(n-1)!} e^{-\lambda t},\, n\in \Bbb N,\, t\geqslant 0, \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: The Erlang density $\psi(t)=\lambda^n t^{n-1}e^{-\lambda t}/(n-1)!$, the law of a sum of $n$ i.i.d. exponentials.
nodes.genus: a sum of $n$ independent exponential variables
differentia: generalizes the exponential density in a natural way

nodes.name: Mean exit times $T_b(x,r)$ and $\TT_b(x)$
nodes.statement: To this end let $r+\mathbf{t}_b^{x,r}$ be the first time past $r$ at which $X_t$ exits $(0,b)$; $T_{b}(x,r)$ be its expected value: $T_{b}(x,r) =\EE[\mathbf{t}_b^{x,r}]$; finally let $\TT_{b}(x) $ denote the mean exit time off $(0,b)$ after a jump $t_n$ (loosely one has $\TT_{b}(x)=T_{b}(x,t_n), n=0,\dots, \infty$; however the relation between both quantities is not trivial, as we see below in Section~\ref{S_up}).
nodes.statement_short: $T_b(x,r)$ is the mean exit time from $(0,b)$ given the present state, $\TT_b(x)$ the mean exit time measured right after a jump.
nodes.genus: the mean exit time off $(0,b)$ after a jump $t_n$

nodes.name: Independence of $r$ holds only in the exponential Markov case
nodes.statement: In the exponential Markov case $ \mathbf{t}_b^{x,r}$ is independent of $r$, $T_{b}(x,r)=\TT_{b}(x)$ and it \it only \rm remains to formulate (and solve) the equation that this object satisfies. However this situation no longer holds in the generic, non-Markovian case where $ \mathbf{t}_b^{x,r}$ does depend on $r$.
nodes.statement_short: Only for exponential holding times is the exit time independent of the present instant $r$.

nodes.name: Excess life $E_r$ and its conditional CDF $\Phi(t|r)$
nodes.statement: We find (see below and Section~\ref{S_up}) that the relation between $T_{b}(x,r)$ and $\TT_{b}(x)$ involves the ``excess life'' $E_r\equiv t_{N_r+1}-r$, or time elapsed until the next arrival occurs. We now sketch classical renewal theory (see \cite{kt81,c65} and \cite{Go}) that shows how to construct the CDF $\Phi(t|r)\equiv \Bbb P\{E_r\leqslant t\}$ of $E_r$.
nodes.statement_short: The excess life $E_r=t_{N_r+1}-r$ is the time from the present until the next arrival; $\Phi(t|r)$ is its CDF.
nodes.genus: time elapsed until the next arrival occurs

nodes.name: Renewal function $m(t)$
nodes.statement: Let $m(t)\equiv \EE[N_t]$ be the mean number of jumps up to $t$: the renewal function.
nodes.genus: the mean number of jumps up to $t$

nodes.name: Integral renewal equation for $m(t)$
nodes.statement: It satisfies the integral renewal equation \begin{equation} m(t)= \Psi(t) +\int_0^t m(t-t')\psi(t')d t'. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: The renewal function solves $m=\Psi+m*\psi$.
assumptions: Let $m(t)\equiv \EE[N_t]$ be the mean number of jumps up to $t$: the renewal function

nodes.name: Excess-life CDF in terms of the renewal function
nodes.statement: Then, by using the total probability theorem it can be proved that \begin{equation} \Phi(t|r) = \int^{r+ t }_{r}\left[1- \Psi(r+ t-t')\right]d m(t'). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: The excess-life CDF is obtained by integrating the survival function against the renewal measure.
assumptions: by using the total probability theorem

nodes.name: Laplace transform $\hat g(s)$
nodes.statement: Let $\hat g(s)$ be the Laplace transform of a function $g(t)$ so that \begin{equation} g(t) =\frac{1}{2\pi i} \int_{c-i\infty}^{c+i\infty} e^{ st} \hat g(s) d s,\ c>0. \end{equation}
nodes.genus: the Laplace transform of a function $g(t)$

nodes.name: Laplace-domain solution for the excess-life distribution
nodes.statement: Then, Eqs. (\ref{re}) and (\ref{repp}) allow to recover the distribution of $E_r$ in closed form via \begin{subequations} \begin{eqnarray} \hat m(s)&=&\frac{1}{s} \frac{\hat\psi(s)}{1-\hat \psi(s)}, \\ \hat \phi(s|r)&=& e^{s r } \left[1-\hat \psi(s)\right] \int_r^\infty e^{-sl} \hat m(l)l d l, \end{eqnarray} \end{subequations} where $ \hat m(s) $ and $ \hat \phi(s|r)$ are the Laplace transforms of $m(t)$ and $\phi(t|r) \equiv \p_t \Phi(t|r)$.
nodes.statement_short: Laplace transformation of the renewal equations gives $\hat m(s)$ and $\hat\phi(s|r)$ in closed form.
assumptions: where $ \hat m(s) $ and $ \hat \phi(s|r)$ are the Laplace transforms of $m(t)$ and $\phi(t|r) \equiv \p_t \Phi(t|r)$
conclusions: \hat \phi(s|r)&=& e^{s r } \left[1-\hat \psi(s)\right] \int_r^\infty e^{-sl} \hat m(l)l d l,

nodes.name: Drift-less relation between $\TT_b(x)$ and $T_b(x,r)$
nodes.statement: If $v=0$ these expressions can be used to relate $T_{b}(x,r) $ and $\TT_{b}(x)$. Indeed let $t_{N_r}\eq t_n$, say, be the ``last'' jump time and $E_r^- \equiv r- t_n$ the time elapsed from $t_n$ to the present. Then, with $E_r^+\equiv E_r$ one obviously has that $E_r^-+E_r^+=t_{n+1}-t_n\equiv\tau_{n+1}$, and that the exit time right after $t_n$ is that after $r$, $\mathbf{t}_b^{x,r}$, plus $E_r^-$, and hence \begin{equation}\TT_{b}(x)=\EE [E_r^-]+ \EE[\mathbf{t}_b^{x,r}]=\EE[\tau_{n+1}]-\EE[E_r^+]+ T_{b}(x,r). \end{equation} Thus, $T_{b}(x,r) $ follows adding a correction term to $\TT_{b}(x)$ which depends only on $r$.
nodes.statement_short: For $v=0$ the two mean exit times differ by $\EE[\tau_{n+1}]-\EE[E_r^+]$, a correction depending only on $r$.
assumptions: If $v=0$
let $t_{N_r}\eq t_n$, say, be the ``last'' jump time and $E_r^- \equiv r- t_n$ the time elapsed from $t_n$ to the present

nodes.name: Failure of the simple argument when $v\neq 0$
nodes.statement: Unfortunately when $v\ne 0$ this simple argument fails as then \it knowledge of the present position does not entail its knowledge at $t_n$\rm. In the next sections we derive the relevant correction to the mean exit time. This correction depends now in all parameters $r$, $x$ and $b$ |see Eqs.~(\ref{Tb_up}) and~(\ref{Tb_down}) below.
nodes.statement_short: With drift, knowing the present position no longer determines the position at the last jump, so the correction depends on $r$, $x$ and $b$.

nodes.name: Renewal argument for the favorable-drift exit-time equation
nodes.statement: Let us assume that at time $t=r$ the system is in $X_r=x\in(0,b)$, and that the excess life $E_r$ is known in advance, $E_r=l$. If the excess life is longer than $\varrho \equiv {b-x\over v}< l$, the drift will drive the process out of the region at time $r+\varrho$, before the next jump takes place at $t_{N_r+1}$. Conversely, if $l \leqslant \varrho$ at least a jump of size $J_{N_r+1}=u$ will occur prior to exiting the interval. Note that just before $t_{N_r+1}$ the process $X_t$ is no longer at $x$, but at $x+v l$. Therefore, two possible scenarios appear: either the jump size is larger than the remaining distance up to the upper boundary, $u\geqslant b-x-v l$, and the process leaves the interval at $r+E_r$, or it does not. In the latter case the problem renews from $t=r+l$, $X_{r+l}=x+v l+u$, so the mean escape time will be increased by an amount $\TT_b\left(x+v l+u\right)$.
nodes.statement_short: Condition on the excess life and on the first jump size, then renew the problem after that jump.

nodes.name: Set up the state and the excess life
nodes.statement: Let us assume that at time $t=r$ the system is in $X_r=x\in(0,b)$, and that the excess life $E_r$ is known in advance, $E_r=l$.
nodes.statement_short: Condition on the present position $x$ and on the excess life $E_r=l$.

nodes.name: Case: excess life exceeds the drift time to the boundary
nodes.statement: If the excess life is longer than $\varrho \equiv {b-x\over v}< l$, the drift will drive the process out of the region at time $r+\varrho$, before the next jump takes place at $t_{N_r+1}$.
nodes.statement_short: If $l>\varrho$ the drift alone carries the process out at time $r+\varrho$.

nodes.name: Case: a jump occurs before the drift exit
nodes.statement: Conversely, if $l \leqslant \varrho$ at least a jump of size $J_{N_r+1}=u$ will occur prior to exiting the interval. Note that just before $t_{N_r+1}$ the process $X_t$ is no longer at $x$, but at $x+v l$.
nodes.statement_short: If $l\leqslant\varrho$ a jump of size $u$ occurs first, from the drifted position $x+vl$.

nodes.name: Sub-case split on the jump size
nodes.statement: Therefore, two possible scenarios appear: either the jump size is larger than the remaining distance up to the upper boundary, $u\geqslant b-x-v l$, and the process leaves the interval at $r+E_r$, or it does not.
nodes.statement_short: Split on whether the jump alone clears the remaining distance $b-x-vl$.

nodes.name: Renew the problem after an interior jump
nodes.statement: In the latter case the problem renews from $t=r+l$, $X_{r+l}=x+v l+u$, so the mean escape time will be increased by an amount $\TT_b\left(x+v l+u\right)$.
nodes.statement_short: If the process stays inside, restart the problem at $x+vl+u$, adding $\TT_b(x+vl+u)$.

nodes.name: Integral equation for $T_b(x,r)$ with favorable drift
nodes.statement: It can be proven that these considerations imply that $T_b(x,r)$ must satisfy |recall that $\psi(\cdot)$, $h(\cdot)$ are the waiting-time and, respectively, jump PDFs| the following equation \begin{eqnarray} T_b(x,r)=\left[1-\Phi\left(\varrho|r\right)\right] \varrho + \int^{\varrho}_{0} l \phi(l|r) \int^{\infty}_{b-x-v l} h(u) d ud l\nonumber \\ +\int^{\varrho}_{0} \phi(l|r) \int^{b-x-v l}_{0} h(u) \left[l+\TT_b\left(x+vl+u\right)\right]d ud l, \end{eqnarray} an expression that relates $T_b(x,r)$ and $\TT_b(x)$. Note that since $\Phi\left(l|r\right)$ depends on $r$ so it does the mean time $T_b(x,r)$. Finally, after some rearrangement, Eq.~(\ref{Tb_up0}) can be conveniently written as \begin{eqnarray} T_b(x,r)= \int^{\varrho}_{0}\left[1-\Phi\left(l|r\right)\right]d l \nonumber \\+ \frac{1}{v}\int^{v \varrho}_{0} \phi\left(\left.\varrho-\frac{z}{v}\right|r\right) \int^{z}_{0} h(u) \TT_b\left(b-z+u\right)d u d z. \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: $T_b(x,r)$ obeys a renewal integral equation coupling it to $\TT_b$, rearranged into a convolution form.
assumptions: recall that $\psi(\cdot)$, $h(\cdot)$ are the waiting-time and, respectively, jump PDFs
conclusions: T_b(x,r)=\left[1-\Phi\left(\varrho|r\right)\right] \varrho + \int^{\varrho}_{0} l \phi(l|r) \int^{\infty}_{b-x-v l} h(u) d ud l\nonumber \\ +\int^{\varrho}_{0} \phi(l|r) \int^{b-x-v l}_{0} h(u) \left[l+\TT_b\left(x+vl+u\right)\right]d ud l,

T_b(x,r)= \int^{\varrho}_{0}\left[1-\Phi\left(l|r\right)\right]d l \nonumber \\+ \frac{1}{v}\int^{v \varrho}_{0} \phi\left(\left.\varrho-\frac{z}{v}\right|r\right) \int^{z}_{0} h(u) \TT_b\left(b-z+u\right)d u d z.

nodes.name: Integral equation for $\TT_b(x)$ with favorable drift
nodes.statement: Similarly, by letting $r\to 0$, we find that $\TT_b(x)$ must satisfy \begin{eqnarray} \TT_b(x)= \int^{\varrho}_{0}\left[1-\Psi(l)\right]d l \nonumber \\ +\frac{1}{v}\int^{v \varrho}_{0} \psi\left(\varrho-\frac{z}{v}\right) \int^{z}_{0} h(u) \TT_b\left(b-z+u\right)d ud z, \end{eqnarray} $x\in(0,b)$.
nodes.statement_short: Letting $r\to 0$ gives the closed integral equation satisfied by the post-jump mean exit time $\TT_b(x)$.
assumptions: by letting $r\to 0$

nodes.name: Allied object $\FF(y)$
nodes.statement: To this end we define the allied object $\FF(y)$, as the solution of the following integral equation \begin{eqnarray} \FF(y)= \int^{y/v}_{0}\left[1-\Psi(l)\right]d l \nonumber \\ +\frac{1}{v}\int^{y}_{0} \psi\left(\frac{y-z}{v}\right) \int^{z}_{0} h(u) \FF\left(z-u\right)d ud z, \end{eqnarray} for $y\in \RR^{+}$.
nodes.statement_short: $\FF(y)$ is defined as the solution of the space-homogeneous version of the $\TT_b$ integral equation.
nodes.genus: the solution of the following integral equation

nodes.name: Closed-form Laplace solution $\hat{\FF}(s)$ for the mean exit time after a jump
nodes.statement: Then it follows that $\TT_b(x) =\FF(b-x)$, for $x\in (0,b)$. We note further that taking a Laplace transformation in Eq.~(\ref{FF_eq}) we find that \begin{equation} \hat{\FF}(s)= \frac{1}{v s^2}\frac{1-\hat{\psi}(s v)}{1-\hat{\psi}(s v)\hat{h}(s)}, \end{equation} where $\hat{\FF}(s)\equiv \int^{\infty}_{0} \FF(y) e^{-s y}d y$, $\hat{h}(s)\equiv \int^{\infty}_{0} h(u) e^{-s u}d u$, and $\hat{\psi}(s)\equiv \int^{\infty}_{0} \psi(s) e^{-s t}d t$. Here $s=s_R+is_I$ is complex and $s_R\geqslant 0$.
nodes.statement_short: With favorable drift, $\TT_b(x)=\FF(b-x)$ and $\hat\FF(s)$ is an explicit rational expression in $\hat\psi$ and $\hat h$.
assumptions: Here $s=s_R+is_I$ is complex and $s_R\geqslant 0$

nodes.name: Closed-form correction $\hat J(s|r)$ for an arbitrary present time
nodes.statement: Further, we also have \begin{equation} \hat{J}(s|r) = \hat{\FF}(s)- \frac{ 1- \hat{h}(s) }{v s^2\left[1-\hat{\psi}(s v)\hat{h}(s)\right]}\left[\hat{\phi}(s v|r)-\hat{\psi}(s v )\right], \end{equation} where the correction to the mean time after a jump is clearly displayed and again, for convenience, we defined $J(y|r)\eq T_b(b-y|r)$, and extended (\ref{Tb_up}) to $y\geqslant 0$. Thus ${\FF}(y) $ and $J(y|r)$ can be recovered by Laplace inversion, cf. Eq.~(\ref{def_m}), and $\TT_b(x)$ and $T_b(x|r)$ will eventually follow.
nodes.statement_short: The Laplace transform of the exit time at an arbitrary present $r$ equals $\hat\FF(s)$ plus an explicit non-Markovian correction.
assumptions: for convenience, we defined $J(y|r)\eq T_b(b-y|r)$, and extended (\ref{Tb_up}) to $y\geqslant 0$

nodes.name: Small-drift expansion of $\hat J(s|r)$
nodes.statement: We first consider the situation when $v$ is small. Let $\mu\equiv~\EE[\tau_{n+1}]$, $\mu_r\equiv~\EE[E_{r}]$; then, using that $ \hat{\psi}(s v )=1-\mu sv +O(v^2)$ and so forth we see that for small $v$, $\hat{ J}(s|r)$ has an expansion in powers of $v$ as \begin{equation} \hat{J}(s|r) = \hat{\FF}(s) - \frac{\mu-\mu_r}{s} - \frac{ \hat{h}(s) }{ 1- \hat{h}(s) } (\mu-\mu_r)\mu v + O(v^2), \end{equation} which implies, in particular, Eq.~(\ref{v=0}).
nodes.statement_short: Expanding in powers of $v$ recovers the drift-less relation at leading order plus an $O(v)$ correction.
assumptions: Let $\mu\equiv~\EE[\tau_{n+1}]$, $\mu_r\equiv~\EE[E_{r}]$
using that $ \hat{\psi}(s v )=1-\mu sv +O(v^2)$ and so forth

nodes.name: Steady-state ($r\to\infty$) mean exit time
nodes.statement: Another interesting case is obtained letting $r\to\infty$: the steady-state solution. This limit is relevant since it can be associated to a situation in which \it the only information available to the observer is the present value of the stochastic process, not even the starting point\rm. Recalling that by the renewal theorem $\un{t\to\infty}\lim m(t)/t = 1/\mu$, Eqs.~(\ref{hat_phi}) and~(\ref{hattime}) yield \begin{eqnarray} \hat\phi (s|\infty) &=& \frac{1-\hat \psi(s)}{s\mu}, \\ \hat{J}(s|\infty) &=& \hat{\FF}(s)- \frac{ 1- \hat{h}(s) }{v^2 s^3 \mu} \frac{1-(1+s v\mu)\hat \psi(sv)}{ 1-\hat{\psi}(s v)\hat{h}(s)}. \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: As $r\to\infty$ the excess life reaches its stationary law and $\hat J(s|\infty)$ takes an explicit form.
assumptions: Recalling that by the renewal theorem $\un{t\to\infty}\lim m(t)/t = 1/\mu$

nodes.name: Exponential jumps and Erlang-2 sojourn times: $\TT_b(x)$
nodes.statement: We illustrate the ideas above by detailing the case when jump magnitudes have an exponential distribution $h(u)=\gamma e^{-\gamma u}$, where $\gamma>0$ is a real parameter, and sojourn times an Erlang distribution $\tau_n\sim\mathcal Er(\lambda,2)$. Hence \begin{equation} \hat{h}(s)= \frac{\gamma}{\gamma +s},\quad \hat{\psi}(s) = \frac{\lambda^2}{(\lambda +s)^2}. \end{equation} In this case Eq.~(\ref{FF_eq}) yields that $\hat{\FF}(s)$ is the following rational function \begin{equation} \hat{\FF}(s)=\frac{1}{v s^2}\frac{2\lambda \gamma v+ v(2 \lambda +\gamma v) s + v^2 s^2}{\lambda (\lambda + 2\gamma v) + v(2 \lambda +\gamma v) s+v^2 s^2}. \end{equation} Hence, the mean escape time of $(0,b)$ after a jump is \begin{eqnarray} \TT_b(x)= \frac{2 \gamma v}{\lambda + 2 \gamma v} \varrho \nonumber\\ +\frac{\lambda^2}{\zrp-\zrm}\left[\frac{1-e^{-\zrm \varrho}}{\zrm^2}-\frac{1-e^{-\zrp \varrho}}{\zrp^2}\right], \end{eqnarray} where we recall that $v \varrho=b-x$ is the initial distance to the boundary $b$ and \begin{equation} z_{\pm}\equiv \lambda +\frac{\gamma v}{2}\left(1\pm\sqrt{1-\frac{4\lambda}{\gamma v}}\right), \end{equation} with $\mbox{Re}[z_{\pm}]>0$.
nodes.statement_short: For $h(u)=\gamma e^{-\gamma u}$ and $\mathcal Er(\lambda,2)$ sojourn times, $\hat\FF$ is rational and $\TT_b(x)$ is a sum of two exponentials in $\varrho$.

nodes.name: Drift time to the boundary $\varrho$
nodes.statement: we recall that $v \varrho=b-x$ is the initial distance to the boundary $b$

nodes.name: Erlang-2 renewal function, excess-life CDF and $T_b(x,r)$
nodes.statement: The evaluation of the mean exit time starting at $r$, $T_b(x,r)$, involves the renewal function and excess-life distribution. We first obtain from Eq.~(\ref{hat_phi}) \begin{equation} \hat m(s)=\frac{\lambda^2}{s^2(2\lambda +s)}, \quad \hat \phi(s|r)=\hat \psi(s)+ \frac{ (1-e^{-2 \lambda r})s\lambda }{ 2 (\lambda +s)^2}. \end{equation} By inversion we get $m(t)= \big(2 \lambda t + e^{-2 \lambda t}-1\big)/4$ and \begin{equation} \ \Phi(t|r) = 1-e^{-\lambda t} \left[ 1+ \left(\frac{ 1+{e^{-2 \lambda r }}}{2}\right)\lambda t \right]. \end{equation} Then by using Eq.~(\ref{hattime}) we find at last that \begin{eqnarray} T_b(x,r) =\TT_b(x) \nonumber \\ - \frac{\lambda}{2}\frac{1-e^{-2\lambda r}}{\zrp-\zrm}\left[\frac{1-e^{-\zrm \varrho}}{\zrm}-\frac{1-e^{-\zrp \varrho}}{\zrp}\right]. \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: Inverting $\hat m$ and $\hat\phi$ for Erlang-2 times yields $\Phi(t|r)$ and an explicit $r$-dependent correction to $\TT_b(x)$.

nodes.name: Drift-less limit of the Erlang-2 mean exit times
nodes.statement: Finally note how, in particular, if $v=0$ then \begin{eqnarray} \TT_b(x)=\frac{2}{\lambda}\left[1+\gamma (b-x)\right] &=& \EE[\tau_n] \left(1+ \frac{b-x}{\EE[J_n]}\right), \\ T_{b}(x,r)&=&\TT_b(x) -\frac{1- e^{-2\lambda r}}{2\la}.\end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: At $v=0$ the Erlang-2 exit times reduce to $\EE[\tau_n](1+(b-x)/\EE[J_n])$ with an exponentially decaying $r$-correction.

nodes.name: Cramer-Lundberg model
nodes.statement: The resulting process is a prototype model in risk management to describe the dynamics of the cahsflow $X_t$ at an insurance company under the assumption that premiums are received at a constant rate $v>0$ and that the company incurs in losses $J_n<0$ from claims reported at times $t_n, n=1,\dots\infty$ (the Cramer-Lundberg model).
nodes.statement_short: An insurance cash-flow model: premiums accrue at constant rate $v>0$ while claims produce negative jumps.

nodes.name: Renewal argument for the opposite-sign exit-time equations
nodes.statement: As before, we analyze the evolution starting at $t=r$ with $X_r=x$. Then if $E_r=l$, $l > \varrho$, the drift will drive the process out of the region through the {\it upper boundary\/} at time $r+\varrho$. Otherwise ($l \leqslant \varrho$) at least a jump $J_{N_r+1}=-u$, say, occurs at time $t_{N_r+1}$ before escape, and two possible scenarios appear depending on the relative magnitudes of the jump size and the location of the process right before the jump, $X_t=x+v l$: for $u\geqslant x+v l$ the process will leave the interval through the {\it lower boundary\/} at $r+E_r$, but when $u<x+v l$ the process after the jump will remain inside the interval, $X_{r+l}=x+v l-u$, the exit problem will start afresh, and the mean escape time will be increased by $\TT_b\left(x+v l-u\right)$.
nodes.statement_short: Same conditioning as before, but now the jump may push the process out through the lower boundary.

nodes.name: No closed-form solution for arbitrary PDFs in the opposite-sign case
nodes.statement: Hence $T_b(x,r)$ follows in terms of quadratures also in this case, given $\TT_b(x)$. Unfortunately, unlike what happens for the case considered in the previous Section, Eq.~(\ref{TTb_down}) can not be solved in closed form for arbitrary PDFs $\psi(\cdot)$ and $h(\cdot)$.
nodes.statement_short: Unlike the favorable-drift case, the opposite-sign equation is not solvable in closed form for general $\psi$ and $h$.

nodes.name: Integro-differential equation for $\TT_b(x)$ with Erlang-2 sojourn times
nodes.statement: Further progress can be made for Erlang times, $\mathcal Er(\lambda,2)$. Indeed, in this case (\ref{TTb_down}) reads \begin{eqnarray} \TT_b(x)= \frac{2-\left(2+\lambda \varrho\right)e^{-\lambda \varrho}}{\lambda} \nonumber \\+\frac{\lambda^2}{v^2} \int^{b}_{x} \left(z-x\right)e^{-\lambda \left(z-x\right)/v} \int^{z}_{0} h(u) \TT_b\left(z-u\right)d ud z, \end{eqnarray} and hence, by differentiation we find that $ \TT_b(x)$, for $0< x< b$, also satisfies the following integral-differential equation: \begin{eqnarray} \TT_b''(x)-\frac{2\lambda}{v}\TT_b'(x)+\frac{\lambda^2}{v^2}\TT_b(x)= \frac{2\lambda}{v^2} \nonumber \\+\frac{\lambda^2}{v^2}\int^{x}_{0}h(u) \TT_b\left(x-u\right)d u, \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: For Erlang-2 waiting times, differentiating the integral equation yields a second-order integro-differential equation for $\TT_b$.

assumptions: for Erlang times, $\mathcal Er(\lambda,2)$
for $0< x< b$, also satisfies

nodes.name: Boundary conditions at $x=b$
nodes.statement: subject to the following boundary conditions: \begin{equation} \lim_{x\to b}\TT_b(x)=0,\mbox{ and }\lim_{x\to b}\TT_b'(x)=-1/v. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: $\TT_b(b)=0$ and $\TT_b'(b)=-1/v$ in the limit $x\to b$.
nodes.section: The case of opposite drift and jumps

nodes.name: Laplace solution of the integro-differential equation in terms of $A$ and $B$
nodes.statement: We first consider a general solution to this equation extending it to the full real axis, so we will drop the subscript in $\TT_b(x)$. We find a solution by Laplace transformation as \begin{eqnarray} \hat{ \TT }(s)= \frac{2\lambda/s + (B v-2 \lambda A)v + A v^2s}{\lambda^2[1-\hat{h}(s)]-2\lambda v s+ v^2s^2}, \end{eqnarray} where $A $ and $B$ are $\TT(0)$ and $\TT'(0)$ respectively. By inversion, cf. Eq.~(\ref{def_m}), $\TT(x)$ follows in terms of $A$ and $B$. By requiring~(\ref{boundary}) we obtain a linear algebraic system for $A$ and $B$, which upon solution yields $\TT_b(x)$ in closed form.
nodes.statement_short: Laplace transforming gives $\hat\TT(s)$ with two unknown constants fixed by the boundary conditions.

nodes.name: Constants $\tilde A$, $\tilde B$ not transcribed
nodes.statement: Unfortunately the final expressions for $\tilde A$ and $\tilde B$ after imposing~(\ref{boundary}) are not very illuminating so we do not transcribe them here. Sampling values for different parameter specifications can be found in Fig.~\ref{E2_down}.
nodes.statement_short: The explicit constants fixed by the boundary conditions are omitted as unilluminating; numerics are shown in a figure.

nodes.name: Ruin-type limit $\TT_\infty(x)$
nodes.statement: The limit $b\to \infty$ is interesting as $\TT_\infty(x)$ gives the probability that $X_t$ ever hits $0$. This corresponds to the classical ruin probability in an insurance context. It turns out that $\TT_\infty(x)$ can be determined in a direct way that avoids solving the aforementioned linear system. Without proof~\footnote{We elaborate on a similar expression in the next section.} we note that if $\lambda > 2 \gamma v $ then \begin{equation} \TT_\infty(x)=\frac{2(1+\gamma x)}{\lambda-2 \gamma v}= \left( 1+\gamma x \right)\Big/\left( \frac{1}{ \Bbb E[\tau_n]}- \frac{v}{ \Bbb E[J_n]} \right), \end{equation} while $\TT_\infty(x)=\infty$ otherwise.
nodes.statement_short: If $\lambda>2\gamma v$ the $b\to\infty$ mean exit time is $2(1+\gamma x)/(\lambda-2\gamma v)$; otherwise it is infinite.
nodes.section: The case of opposite drift and jumps
assumptions: $\lambda > 2 \gamma v $

nodes.name: Renewal argument for the two-sided exit-time equations
nodes.statement: The relevant analysis is similar to that of the last section if one incorporates the possibility of an upper exit due to a jump: If $E_r=l>\varrho$ the drift drives directly the process through the upper boundary. If $l\leqslant \varrho$ at least a jump occurs before the exit of the process. When the size $u$ of this jump is positive and $u\geqslant b-x-vl$ the process leaves the interval at time $r+E_r$ through the upper boundary, when $u\leqslant -(x+vl)<0$ the exit takes place through the lower boundary, otherwise the process remains inside the interval $(0,b)$ and the problem restarts.
nodes.statement_short: Repeat the conditioning argument allowing a jump to exit through either boundary.

nodes.name: Adapt the previous argument to two-sided jumps
nodes.statement: The relevant analysis is similar to that of the last section if one incorporates the possibility of an upper exit due to a jump:
nodes.statement_short: Reuse the previous case analysis, adding the possibility of an upward jump exit.

nodes.name: Case: drift exit before any jump
nodes.statement: If $E_r=l>\varrho$ the drift drives directly the process through the upper boundary.
nodes.statement_short: If $l>\varrho$ the drift alone produces an upper exit.

nodes.name: Case: a jump occurs before the exit
nodes.statement: If $l\leqslant \varrho$ at least a jump occurs before the exit of the process.
nodes.statement_short: If $l\leqslant\varrho$ a jump precedes the exit.

nodes.name: Three-way split on the sign and size of the jump
nodes.statement: When the size $u$ of this jump is positive and $u\geqslant b-x-vl$ the process leaves the interval at time $r+E_r$ through the upper boundary, when $u\leqslant -(x+vl)<0$ the exit takes place through the lower boundary, otherwise the process remains inside the interval $(0,b)$ and the problem restarts.
nodes.statement_short: A large positive jump exits above, a jump below $-(x+vl)$ exits below, otherwise the problem restarts.

nodes.name: Integral equations for two-sided jumps
nodes.statement: Skipping minor details we obtain that $\TT_b(x)$ and $T_b(x,r)$ satisfy respectively \begin{eqnarray} T_b(x,r)= \int^{\varrho}_{0}\left[1-\Phi\left(l|r\right)\right]d l \nonumber \\+ \frac{1}{v}\int^{b}_{x} \phi\left(\left.\frac{z-x}{v}\right|r\right) \int^{b-z}_{-z} h(u) \TT_b\left(z+u\right)d ud z, \end{eqnarray} and \begin{eqnarray} \TT_b(x)= \int^{\varrho}_{0}\left[1-\Psi\left(l\right)\right]d l \nonumber \\+ \frac{1}{v}\int^{b}_{x} \psi\left(\frac{z-x}{v}\right) \int^{b-z}_{-z} h(u) \TT_b\left(z+u\right)dud z. \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: For jumps of either sign both mean exit times satisfy integral equations with the inner jump integral running over $(-z,b-z)$.

nodes.name: General two-sided equation is not solvable in closed form
nodes.statement: In a general situation, the latter integral equation is not solvable in closed form.
nodes.statement_short: No closed-form solution is available for the general two-sided integral equation.

nodes.name: Decomposition of the jump PDF $h=q h_+ + p h_-$
nodes.statement: To gain some insight we use the decomposition $ h(x)= q h_+(x) + p h_-(x)$ where $p$ is the probability that a given jump be negative, $q\equiv 1-p$ and $h_{\pm}(\cdot)$ are the jump PDF in the positive/negative regions, i.e. $h_+(x)\equiv h(x) \theta(x) \big/ q$, say.
nodes.statement_short: Split the jump density into positive and negative parts with weights $q=1-p$ and $p$.
nodes.genus: the jump PDF in the positive/negative regions

nodes.name: Vanishing negative part recovers the favorable-drift case
nodes.statement: Note that if $h_-(x)=0, \fo x\leqslant 0$, we recover the case considered in Section~\ref{S_up}, solvable via Laplace transformation.
nodes.statement_short: If the negative part of the jump density vanishes identically one is back in the solvable favorable-drift setting.

nodes.name: Closed solution when $h_-$ vanishes only on $(-b,0)$
nodes.statement: It turns out that we can still \it construct an analytic closed solution \rm in the more general case when $h_-(x) $ vanishes \it only \rm on $(-b,0)$ |but not on $(-\infty,-b]$. In such a case a negative jump will drive the process out of the interval $(0,b)$ through the lower boundary. Thus $p$ is related to the ruin risk in a economic scenario or to the breakdown probability in a physical system. The equation for $\TT_b(x)$ reads in this case \begin{eqnarray} \TT_b(x)= \int^{\varrho}_{0}\left[1-\Psi\left(l\right)\right]d l \nonumber\\+ \frac{q}{v}\int^{b}_{x} \psi\left(\frac{z-x}{v}\right) \int^{b-z}_{0} h_+(u) \TT_b\left(z+u\right)d ud z, \end{eqnarray} while a similar expression, with $\phi(\cdot|r)$ in place of $\psi(\cdot)$, holds for $T_b(x,r)$.
nodes.statement_short: If every negative jump is large enough to exit below, $\TT_b$ obeys the favorable-drift equation with an extra factor $q$.
assumptions: when $h_-(x) $ vanishes \it only \rm on $(-b,0)$ |but not on $(-\infty,-b]$

nodes.name: Resemblance to the favorable-drift equations
nodes.statement: Note that these equations are independent of the form of $h_-(\cdot)$ and apart from the factor $q$ in front of the second term they resemble Eqs.~(\ref{Tb_up}) and~(\ref{TTb_up}); it follows that we can resort to the same technique used in Section~\ref{S_up}:
nodes.statement_short: Apart from the factor $q$ the equations coincide with those of the favorable-drift section, so the same Laplace technique applies.

nodes.name: Auxiliary equation and $\hat{\FF}(s)$ for the ruin-type two-sided case
nodes.statement: We consider \begin{eqnarray} \FF(y)= \int^{y/v}_{0}\left[1-\Psi(l)\right]d l \nonumber \\+ \frac{q}{v}\int^{y}_{0} \psi\left(\frac{y-z}{v}\right) \int^{z}_{0} h(u) \FF\left(z-u\right)d ud z, \end{eqnarray} for $y\in \RR^{+}$ which is again solvable by means of a Laplace transform; then $\TT_b(x)$ follows from $\TT_b(x) =\FF(b-x)$ for $x\in (0,b)$. With the previous selection for $h(\cdot)$ and $\psi(\cdot)$, Eq.~(\ref{h_hat}), and in terms of $z=sv $ we find \begin{eqnarray} \hat{\FF}(s)=\frac{v}{z} \frac{2\lambda \gamma v + (2 \lambda+\gamma v ) z + z^2}{p \lambda^2 \gamma v + \lambda (\lambda +2\gamma v ) z+ (2 \lambda +\gamma v ) z^2+z^3 }. \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: The $q$-weighted auxiliary equation is again Laplace-solvable, giving a rational $\hat\FF(s)$ with a cubic denominator.
assumptions: With the previous selection for $h(\cdot)$ and $\psi(\cdot)$, Eq.~(\ref{h_hat}), and in terms of $z=sv $
conclusions: \hat{\FF}(s)=\frac{v}{z} \frac{2\lambda \gamma v + (2 \lambda+\gamma v ) z + z^2}{p \lambda^2 \gamma v + \lambda (\lambda +2\gamma v ) z+ (2 \lambda +\gamma v ) z^2+z^3 }.

nodes.name: Closed-form mean exit time when $\lambda=\gamma v$
nodes.statement: We first consider the case when $\lambda =\gamma v$. Under this assumption $\hat{\FF}(s)$ has poles at $z=z_j\equiv \lambda \left(q^{1/3} e^{2\pi ij/3}-1\right)$, $j\in\{1,2,3\}$, and $z=0$. Inverse Laplace transformation yields the mean exit time as \begin{equation} \TT_b(x)= \frac{2}{ p\lambda}+ \sum_{j=1}^3 \frac{ 1+q^{-1/3} e^{-2\pi ij/3}}{ 3 z_j} e^{z_j\varrho}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: At $\lambda=\gamma v$ the cubic factorizes and $\TT_b(x)$ is a sum of three exponentials plus $2/(p\lambda)$.

nodes.name: Large-$b$ limit of the two-sided mean exit time
nodes.statement: Returning to the general case we see that the inversion of the Laplace transform involves solving a cubic equation, and though explicit formulas are available the resulting expression is awkward. Still, the large $b$ limit can be discerned with all generality. To this end we note that by appealing to Hurwitz's stability criteria it can be proven that all three roots $z_j$, $j\in\{1,2,3\}$, of the denominator in expression (\ref{FF}) |apart from $z=0$| have negative real parts. Hence, evaluating the inversion integral by residues we find \begin{eqnarray} \TT_b(x)=\frac{2}{ p\lambda} + \sum_{j=1}^3C_j e^{z_j\varrho}, \end{eqnarray} where $C_j$ are certain constants. Thus, letting $b\to\infty$ we see that $\TT_b(x) \underset{b \to\infty}\to \frac{2 }{ p\lambda} =\frac{\EE[\tau_n]}{1-\EE[\theta(J_n)]}$.
nodes.statement_short: Hurwitz's criterion makes all three poles stable, so residues give $\TT_b(x)\to 2/(p\lambda)=\EE[\tau_n]/(1-\EE[\theta(J_n)])$ as $b\to\infty$.
assumptions: by appealing to Hurwitz's stability criteria it can be proven that all three roots $z_j$, $j\in\{1,2,3\}$, of the denominator in expression (\ref{FF}) |apart from $z=0$| have negative real parts

nodes.name: Evaluation of the correction to $T_b(x,r)$ in the two-sided case
nodes.statement: The evaluation of the correction to $T_b(x,r)$ does not present particular difficulties. We leave it as an exercise to the interested reader.
nodes.statement_short: Left to the reader: compute the $r$-dependent correction for the two-sided jump process.

nodes.name: Generalization to wider waiting-time distributions and reducibility conditions
nodes.statement: We plan to generalize these ideas to a more general class of waiting-time distributions and pinpoint conditions that guarantee the reducibility of the original formulation to simpler differential equations.
nodes.statement_short: Extend the method beyond Erlang waiting times and characterize when the integral formulation reduces to a differential equation.

nodes.name: Continuum limit
nodes.statement: In particular, we shall stress the connections of both techniques under the continuum limit approximation. This concept |which we will define properly in short| can be loosely identified with the limit in which both the mean sojourn time $\mu$ and the characteristic jump magnitude tend to zero |note that, by contrast, in this paper we have considered a situation wherein sojourn times are moderate or even large.
nodes.statement_short: The limit in which both the mean sojourn time and the characteristic jump size tend to zero.
nodes.section: Some remarks on the continuum limit and its relationship with fractional diffusions
nodes.genus: the limit in which both the mean sojourn time $\mu$ and the characteristic jump magnitude tend to zero

nodes.name: Benefit and drawback of the continuum assumption
nodes.statement: The major benefit of the continuum assumption is that it allows to obtain general results on the basis of limited knowledge of the jumping time and size PDFs, even when these distributions do not have all their moments well defined. The major drawback within our set-up is that as $\mu \to 0$ the variable $r$, the time elapsed from the last known jump, tends to zero as well, and the distinction between $T_b(x,r)$ and $\TT_b(x)$ becomes irrelevant. Therefore, any comparison between the two methods must be focused on how the object $\TT_b(x)$ is obtained.
nodes.statement_short: The continuum limit needs little distributional detail but erases the distinction between $T_b(x,r)$ and $\TT_b(x)$.
nodes.section: Some remarks on the continuum limit and its relationship with fractional diffusions

nodes.name: One-sided stable jump density with $\hat h(s)=e^{-k\sqrt{s}}$
nodes.statement: To be more explicit, let us consider the case \begin{equation} h(u)=\frac{k}{2 \sqrt{\pi u^3}} e^{-\frac{k^2}{4 u}}\quad (u>0), \end{equation} so that, \begin{equation} \hat h(s)=e^{-k \sqrt{s}}\sim 1-k \sqrt{s} +o(\sqrt{s}). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Take the one-sided stable density of index $1/2$, whose Laplace transform is $e^{-k\sqrt s}$.
nodes.section: Some remarks on the continuum limit and its relationship with fractional diffusions

nodes.name: CTRW propagator and its fractional diffusion limit
nodes.statement: It is well known that for the CTRW process $S_t$, Eq.~(\ref{process}), the propagator $p(u,t)du\equiv\Pr\{u<S_t\leqslant u+du\}$ reads in the Laplace-Laplace domain \begin{equation} \hat p(s_1,s_2)= \frac{1}{s_2}\frac{1-\hat{\psi}(s_2)}{1-\hat{\psi}(s_2)\hat{h}(s_1)}\sim\frac{\mu}{\mu s_2+k \sqrt{s_1}}, \end{equation} as $s_{1,2}\to 0$. The continuum limit is recovered in this case by letting $\mu \to 0$, $k \to 0$ with $k/\mu \to K$ finite. The process arising after this limit fulfills the following fractional diffusion equation \begin{equation} \partial_t p(u,t) + K\ { }^{}_0 D_u^{\frac{1}{2}} p(u,t)=0, \end{equation} where ${ }^{}_0 D_u^{\frac{1}{2}}$ is the Riemann-Liouville fractional operator of order $\frac{1}{2}$, and whose solution reads \begin{equation} p(u,t)=\frac{K t}{2 \sqrt{\pi u^3}} e^{-\frac{K^2 t^2}{4 u}}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: The Montroll-Weiss propagator degenerates, under $\mu,k\to0$ with $k/\mu\to K$, into a Riemann-Liouville fractional diffusion equation of order $1/2$.
nodes.section: Some remarks on the continuum limit and its relationship with fractional diffusions
assumptions: The continuum limit is recovered in this case by letting $\mu \to 0$, $k \to 0$ with $k/\mu \to K$ finite
conclusions: p(u,t)=\frac{K t}{2 \sqrt{\pi u^3}} e^{-\frac{K^2 t^2}{4 u}}.

nodes.name: Survival probability $\Pi_b(x,t)$
nodes.statement: Let us now define $\Pi_b(x,t)$ as the probability that the process $X_t$ has never touched $b$ when it started at $x< b$ at the initial time, i.e. \begin{equation} \Pi_b(x,t)\equiv\Pr\{X_{t'}< b, 0\leqslant t' \leqslant t |X_0=x\}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: $\Pi_b(x,t)$ is the probability that the process started at $x<b$ has not touched $b$ by time $t$.
nodes.section: Some remarks on the continuum limit and its relationship with fractional diffusions
nodes.genus: the probability that the process $X_t$ has never touched $b$ when it started at $x< b$ at the initial time

nodes.name: Agreement of the renewal approach with the continuum-limit computation
nodes.statement: Alternatively, if we use the direct approach followed in this paper our results imply that the mean arrival time follows by inversion of the Laplace expression in Eq.~(\ref{FF_sol}) when $\mu \to 0$, $k \to 0$ with $k/\mu \to K$ finite \begin{equation} \hat{\FF}(s)=\frac{1}{v s^2}\frac{1-\hat{\psi}(s v)}{1-\hat{\psi}(s v)\hat{h}(s)} \rightarrow \frac{1}{vs^2 +Ks^{\frac{3}{2}}}, \end{equation} that is \begin{equation} \TT_b(x)=\frac{1}{2\pi i} \int_{c-i\infty}^{c+i\infty} \frac{e^{ s(b-x)} }{vs^2 +Ks^{\frac{3}{2}}} d s. \end{equation} Upon evaluation of this integral the result (\ref{Ex_TTb}) is recovered.
nodes.statement_short: Taking the same limit inside $\hat\FF(s)$ and inverting reproduces the propagator-based formula for $\TT_b(x)$.

assumptions: when $\mu \to 0$, $k \to 0$ with $k/\mu \to K$ finite
